routing.title: Routing
routing.lead: FrontX keeps every screen and every nested occupant in the query string of one shared browser history and leaves the pathname to the shell. Two packages do it: routing owns the history and the address grammar, and routing-tanstack gives each microfrontend its own TanStack Router over its own part of the address.

routing.addressing.title: Query addressing
routing.addressing.lead: The pathname belongs to the shell. Every extension domain is addressed by an entry in the query string.
routing.addressing.example: The routing package's own example, one line in the address bar, wrapped here to read
routing.addressing.reading.1: screen, sheet and widgets are domain keys; dashboard, tenant-details and line-a are the extensions that occupy them; the ;name=value pairs are the occupant's own parameters.
routing.addressing.reading.2: A domain with several occupants contributes one entry for each, all with its domain key: widgets appears three times above.
routing.addressing.reading.3: A domain key and an extension token are names: lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter. The package rejects anything else when you declare it.
routing.addressing.reading.4: A parameter name without = has an empty value, and a name repeated inside one entry is rejected on write.
routing.addressing.reading.5: A query segment that is not an entry, such as an OAuth state or an analytics utm parameter, is kept as it is and written back untouched.
routing.addressing.reading.6: The hash is the application's own and is copied verbatim. Reading an address never throws: a malformed entry is dropped with a warning.
routing.addressing.reading.7: A slash stays readable inside a value: route=settings/general is written as it reads.
routing.packages.title: The two packages
routing.packages.panel.1.title: @gears-frontx/routing
routing.packages.panel.1.text: The navigation substrate. One browser history shared by the host and every independently bundled microfrontend (resolveNavigationHistory), the address codec (parseGrammar, serializeGrammar, validateName) and the route ownership signal (createRouteSignal), which reports which extension owns each entry of a domain and rewrites a domain's own entries in one history write. It depends on no router engine and no UI framework.
routing.packages.panel.2.title: @gears-frontx/routing-tanstack
routing.packages.panel.2.text: FrontX's default routing-engine provider. It projects the one entry a microfrontend was mounted at into a virtual location, builds a TanStack Router over it (createProviderRouter, adaptProviderHistory, EngineProvider) and re-exports the engine's route builders and hooks (createRootRoute, createRoute, Link, Outlet, useNavigate, useParams, useSearch, useRouterState) for a microfrontend's own route tree. It is the only package in the ecosystem that imports a concrete router engine.
routing.inside.title: Pages inside a screen
routing.inside.lead: Inside one screen, the entry's own route parameter is the page path and every other parameter is search.
routing.inside.example: One entry, as the screen's router sees it
routing.inside.rules.1: route is routing-tanstack's own convention, not a rule of the address grammar, which knows entries and parameters only.
routing.inside.rules.2: A page's path is written back only when it is not /.
routing.inside.rules.3: A screen's navigation writes only its own entry: Link, useNavigate and the engine's route hooks work on the screen's virtual location and never touch a sibling's entry, another domain's entry or the shell's part of the address.
routing.inside.rules.4: The same construction runs standalone: with no entry address, the virtual location is the page's own pathname and search.
routing.inside.limits.1: A history entry carries no state: navigate({ state }) and <Link state> are dropped, useLocation().state never holds your value, and route masking does not work.
routing.inside.limits.2: Put what you would have put in state into the search parameters, where it survives a reload and a shared link.
routing.router.title: ExtensionRouter
routing.router.lead: A microfrontend declares a route tree and renders it; it never builds a router itself.
routing.router.example: A screen's route tree and its router
routing.router.rules.1: ExtensionRouter comes from @gears-frontx/react. It resolves the adapted history from the registry's own router, so the screen never imports createProviderRouter, adaptProviderHistory or EngineProvider and never sees its own entry address or the raw history.
routing.router.rules.2: The routing packages are shared dependencies of every microfrontend build on this site, so a screen's route tree and ExtensionRouter use one copy of the router and its React context.
routing.router.rules.3: Code outside the rendered tree, such as an action handler, navigates through the extension-local facade app.mfeRouter.navigation(): navigate(path), replace(path) and location().
routing.router.limits.summary: A route tree with a router context
routing.router.limits.1: ExtensionRouter takes a route tree that declares no router context. A tree built with createRootRouteWithContext needs its own typed call to createProviderRouter, with the context passed as its options.
routing.writer.title: Who writes the address
routing.writer.lead: One party writes it, and only as the result of an action.
routing.writer.rules.1: An occupant enters or leaves the address only as a byproduct of an executed mount_ext or unmount_ext action. The shell, a microfrontend or a host never writes it directly.
routing.writer.rules.2: A cold load, a reload, a back or forward step and an address typed in are translated into the same mount_ext chains with the history intent none, so those chains add nothing to history.
routing.writer.rules.3: The two actions carry an optional history intent, none, replace or push; without one the write is a push.

mfes.title: Microfrontends
mfes.lead: A microfrontend is a separately built package that the host loads at runtime from a published manifest and mounts into an extension domain, in its own Shadow DOM and its own module graph. @gears-frontx/mfes is the runtime that registers, loads, admits, mounts and connects them without knowing what they are.

mfes.declarations.title: What a microfrontend declares
mfes.declarations.lead: Four declarations describe a microfrontend and where it goes. This site's mfe.json files hold them.
mfes.declarations.panel.1.title: Manifest
mfes.declarations.panel.1.text: Package-level metadata: the public path, the remote entry descriptor and the shared dependencies with their chunk paths. In an mfe.json it is the manifest id and the remoteEntry address.
mfes.declarations.panel.2.title: Entry
mfes.declarations.panel.2.text: The entry point and its communication contract: the shared properties the domain must provide (requiredProperties) and may provide (optionalProperties), the actions the entry can receive (actions) and the actions the domain must support (domainActions). A Module Federation entry names its exposed module, which holds the lifecycle.
mfes.declarations.panel.3.title: Extension
mfes.declarations.panel.3.text: Binds an entry to a domain: its id, the domain, the entry, an optional route and optional lifecycle hooks. An extension of the screen domain also carries presentation (label, icon, order), which builds the menu.
mfes.declarations.panel.4.title: Domain
mfes.declarations.panel.4.text: A placement the application registers: the shared properties it provides, the actions it can execute, the actions an entry must support to be placed in it, its lifecycle stages, a default action timeout and an optional route. A mount strategy (Concurrent, Optional or Exclusive) decides how many occupants it holds.
mfes.admission.title: Registration and admission
mfes.admission.lead: The runtime admits an extension only after it passes checks, and fetches its code only when it is first loaded.
mfes.admission.registry: Building the registry of a FrontX application
mfes.admission.rules.1: Registration runs in order: schemas, manifest, domains, entries, extensions. template-shell's bootstrap registers each package's declarations from generated-mfe-manifests.json this way.
mfes.admission.rules.2: Admission matches an extension's entry against the domain's contract, the properties and actions the entry needs against what the domain provides, and the extension's type against the domain's extensionsTypeId. A mismatch rejects the extension.
mfes.admission.rules.3: A domain declares one mount strategy; at registration the runtime checks that the domain's declared actions fit the strategy and rejects the domain if they do not.
mfes.admission.rules.4: Type identifiers are opaque strings to the runtime. An injected type-system provider validates them.
mfes.admission.rules.5: load_ext fetches an extension's bundle without mounting it; mount_ext mounts it.
mfes.admission.rules.6: A registry is built once per runtime: a later build must supply the identical type system and router, or it is rejected.
mfes.lifecycle.title: Lifecycle
mfes.lifecycle.lead: An entry's module exports a lifecycle with two methods, mount and unmount.
mfes.lifecycle.example: A screen's lifecycle in a FrontX React package
mfes.lifecycle.rules.1: mount(container, bridge, mountContext) renders into the container, a ShadowRoot with the default handler, and receives the bridge. The runtime treats the completion of the call as the readiness signal, so it must not finish before the microfrontend has registered its action handlers.
mfes.lifecycle.rules.2: unmount(container) tears the tree down. Action handlers and property subscriptions made through the bridge outlive an unmount and are presented again to the next mount; code that binds them to a UI tree torn down in unmount must release them there, or the next mount delivers twice.
mfes.lifecycle.rules.3: ThemeAwareReactLifecycle from @gears-frontx/react implements both for React: a subclass supplies renderContent(bridge).
mfes.isolation.title: Isolation
mfes.isolation.lead: Two mechanisms keep a microfrontend apart from the host and from its siblings: a Shadow DOM for what it renders and a module graph of its own for what it runs.
mfes.isolation.rules.1: With the default handler each microfrontend renders into its own ShadowRoot, which isolates its styles. The runtime exports createShadowRoot, injectCssVariables and injectStylesheet for handlers.
mfes.isolation.rules.2: Each load builds an isolated module graph covering its whole dependency chain, keyed by the extension's identity: two extensions that share one definition are two separate instances. Where a dependency cycle cannot stay inside the graph, the load fails instead of resolving outside it.
mfes.isolation.rules.3: Dependencies a build externalizes (react and the @gears-frontx packages on this site) are linked by the MFE handler at runtime, and their source text is reused through one bounded cache shared by every load in the page.
mfes.bridge.title: The bridge
mfes.bridge.lead: A microfrontend reaches the host through one narrow object and never through the registry.
mfes.bridge.rules.1: ChildMfeBridge has four methods and two read-only identity properties. Each method delegates to the registry; the bridge adds no coordination of its own.
mfes.bridge.rules.2: While the bridge is inactive it hands nothing over.
mfes.bridge.rules.3: One bridge pair exists per registered extension, and it is the same object at every mount. An unmount deactivates the bridge; it is disposed only when the extension is unregistered.
mfes.bridge.rules.4: The host holds the parent end, which exposes only the extension's id and dispose().
mfes.properties.title: Shared properties
mfes.properties.lead: The host passes values to a microfrontend as shared properties, each named by a type id.
mfes.properties.rules.1: A domain declares the shared properties it provides. An entry lists in requiredProperties those the domain must provide and in optionalProperties those it may; admission fails when a required one is missing.
mfes.properties.rules.2: The microfrontend reads the current value with bridge.getProperty(id) and follows changes with bridge.subscribeToProperty(id, callback). The host changes a value with registry.updateSharedProperty(id, value).
mfes.properties.rules.3: template-shell's screen domain provides two, the theme and the language (FRONTX_SHARED_PROPERTY_THEME and FRONTX_SHARED_PROPERTY_LANGUAGE), and every screen of this site reads them through its bridge.
mfes.actions.title: Actions
mfes.actions.lead: Everything a microfrontend asks of the host, and the host of a microfrontend, is an action sent to a target.
mfes.actions.example: An actions chain that mounts a screen
mfes.actions.rules.1: An action names its type, its target (a domain or an extension) and an optional payload and timeout. The mediator dispatches it to the handler registered for that target and type.
mfes.actions.rules.2: The lifecycle actions are load_ext, mount_ext and unmount_ext; each takes the extension id as payload.subject.
mfes.actions.rules.3: Concrete action schemas are closed: an action with a field its schema does not declare fails admission, and its chain takes the fallback or, without one, ends silently.
mfes.actions.rules.4: A microfrontend answers actions with handlers it registers on its bridge: bridge.registerActionHandler(type, ActionHandler.fromFunction(...)).
mfes.nesting.1: A mounted microfrontend may itself build and host a further registry. Actions then reach targets across the nesting through the bridges that connect adjacent registries, with no change to the bridge a microfrontend holds.

domain.title: Screen domain
domain.lead: The screen domain is the main content area of template-shell: one extension domain whose single occupant is the screen on show. Mounting a screen replaces the previous one, and the screen's token is the screen entry of the address.

domain.what.title: What it is
domain.what.lead: template-shell declares four base domains: screen, sidebar, popup and overlay. The screen domain holds the page content.
domain.what.rules.1: The declaration is screenDomain from @gears-frontx/framework; the shell's bootstrap registers it with its own implementation, which composes the Exclusive mount strategy.
domain.what.rules.2: The domain is a permanent fixture, always visible and never destroyed while the application runs, so it declares only the init lifecycle stage. The screens in it go through init, activated, deactivated and destroyed.
domain.what.rules.3: Its extensions must be of the screen extension type: a screen declares a route and presentation metadata (label, icon, order), and the host builds its menu from them.
domain.what.rules.4: It provides the theme and language shared properties to every screen.
domain.extension.title: A screen is an extension
domain.extension.lead: Each screen of this site is one extension of the screen domain.
domain.extension.example: The Libraries screen's extension, from its mfe.json
domain.extension.rules.1: route is /libs. Stripping the leading slash gives the extension token libs, the value after screen= in the address.
domain.extension.rules.2: A route that is not a valid name (lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter) makes the extension not routable, and it is never written to the address.
domain.extension.rules.3: presentation.order sorts the menu, lower first.
domain.exclusive.title: The Exclusive mount strategy
domain.exclusive.lead: The domain composes ExclusiveMountStrategy: exactly one screen is mounted, and mounting another evicts it first.
domain.exclusive.rules.1: Mounting always evicts whatever else is mounted in the domain before mounting the new extension. There is no public unmount_ext: the domain declares only load_ext and mount_ext, and the cardinality check rejects an Exclusive domain that lists unmount_ext.
domain.exclusive.rules.2: The domain queues requests in two places, the running mount and one pending mount. A further request replaces the pending one, and the replaced request fails and takes its chain's fallback. With A running and B, C and D requested in turn, only A and D are ever mounted.
domain.exclusive.rules.3: A pending request fails when its timer fires before it starts. The timer is the action's timeout or else the domain's default action timeout, 30000 ms here. A request that is already running is never interrupted.
domain.exclusive.rules.4: A mount_ext of the screen already on show succeeds at once while the queue is empty.
domain.exclusive.others.1: sidebar, popup and overlay use the Optional strategy: zero or one occupant. Mounting displaces the occupant and an explicit unmount_ext empties the slot, so they declare load_ext, mount_ext and unmount_ext.
domain.exclusive.others.2: Their route keys are sidebar, popup and overlay.
domain.mount.title: Switching screens: mount_ext
domain.mount.lead: A screen changes when a mount_ext action targets the screen domain.
domain.mount.example: Mounting a screen from a microfrontend
domain.mount.rules.1: payload.subject is the extension id. The optional history field takes none, replace or push; without it the mount is written as a push.
domain.mount.rules.2: Nothing writes the address after a mount: the injected router is told of each settled mount and rewrites the screen entry itself.
domain.mount.rules.3: A reload and a back or forward step run the same mount_ext with the history intent none, so the address is not written again.
domain.mount.rules.4: On this site, a plain click on a link to another screen sends this action on the clicking screen's bridge.
domain.key.title: The route key
domain.key.lead: The domain declares route: 'screen'. That value is the domain key in the address: ?screen=<token>.
domain.key.rules.1: A domain's route is a name in the grammar's alphabet and is unique among the routed domains live in the page; the router rejects a duplicate registration.
domain.key.rules.2: The pathname stays the shell's. Inside the screen, the page is the entry's route parameter, as the routing summary describes.
